name: Manikandeswarar Temple, Tirumalpur
deity: Shiva as Manikandeswarar (Maalvanangeeswarar), with the goddess Karunai Nayaki (Anjanakshi)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple of the Chola period and later
summary: Manikandeswarar is the Shiva temple of Tirumalpur in the Thondai country, a Paadal Petra Sthalam remembered in tradition for Vishnu's worship of Shiva here and for the goddess Parvati's sand linga, raised in atonement on the river bank.

sections.history: Tirumalpur, known in older usage as Tirumarperu, stands in the Thondai country in what is now Ranipet district. The presiding Lord is praised in the Tevaram, where the hymns of the saints Appar and Sambandar name the shrine, which counts it among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the temples sung by the Tamil Shaiva saints. The town's name is read as linked to Tirumal, the name of Vishnu, from a tradition that remembers his worship of Shiva here. The present stone temple belongs to the Chola period and later, raised and enlarged by the patrons of the Tamil country and kept in worship ever since.
sections.architecture: Built in the Dravidian manner and entered beneath a rajagopuram, the temple holds the Shiva linga as Manikandeswarar, who is also called Maalvanangeeswarar, the Lord worshipped by Vishnu. The goddess Karunai Nayaki, also named Anjanakshi, is honoured in her own shrine. Within the enclosure lies the temple tank, remembered as Chakra Theertham, and tradition keeps here a venerated linga of sand on the river bank, covered with a sheath of copper when it is bathed so that the sand may not be disturbed. Sources leave the finer measures of the temple unrecorded, so they are kept general here.
sections.legends: Two stories gather at Tirumalpur. In the first, Vishnu is said to have worshipped Shiva here and to have had his discus, the Sudarshana chakra, restored to its edge, and from his name, Tirumal, the town is called. In the second, the goddess Parvati, in play, covered Shiva's eyes with her hands and so plunged the worlds into darkness; to atone she shaped a linga of sand on the bank of the river and worshipped it, and that sand linga is venerated to this day and shielded by a copper cover during its ablutions. Both are told as the temple's sacred tradition.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the festivals common to the great Shiva shrines, with a car festival and street processions drawing the deities through the town, and Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham observed with devotion. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Tirumalpur rewards an unhurried visit. Come to the sanctum of Manikandeswarar, turn to the compassionate goddess Karunai Nayaki in her own shrine, and walk to the temple tank remembered as Chakra Theertham. Devotees hold dear the tradition of the sand linga and the stories of Vishnu's and Parvati's worship, which give the old shrine its particular feeling of a place where the gods themselves came to pray. The town lies on the plain near Arakkonam, but within the walls the temple keeps the quiet of a very old sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirumalpur is in Ranipet district, in the Arakkonam taluk, with its own station on the Chennai suburban railway line and about 8 km from Thakkolam. Arakkonam and Kanchipuram are the nearest large centres, with frequent buses, and Chennai is the nearest airport. Confirm distances and connections locally.
